1972 Challenger High School Driver Sat 25 Years, Gets New Owner and Engine, Drops Massive Burnouts
83 photos
Photo: YouTube/Dylan McCool
Rescuing a classic American muscle car after decades of slumber requires equal parts mechanical ingenuity, patience, and a healthy dose of stubbornness-infused faith. That’s all it takes, apparently, to make an engineless 1972 Dodge Challenger run and drive from Alabama to Tennessee. Parked inside a barn for 25 years and missing its engine for over 20 years, the Mopar icon proves miracles are real. And perfectly within the grasp of reason.
The story of this 1972 Dodge Challenger began in 1989, when previous owner Eddie Ball purchased the coupe while attending high school. Inspired by his aunt, who owned a triple-black 1972 Challenger rally car powered by a 340 cubic-inch engine that he could not acquire, Ball searched for his own example. An acquaintance soon directed him to this baby blue Challenger in Anderson, Alabama, fulfilling a dream – and setting in motion a chain of events that ended on Dylan McCool’s YouTube channel.
When Ball bought the Dodge, it was a dependable daily driver equipped with a 318 cubic-inch V8, an automatic transmission, and functional air conditioning. He drove the car throughout high school and took it on his senior trip to Panama City, Florida. Roughly two years later, he installed a 1969 model 340 small-block and mounted 4-speed manual pedals, though tight finances and impending fatherhood kept the automatic transmission in place.
The Challenger saw regular road duty until around 2001 or 2002, when another motorist pulled out in front of Ball, damaging the passenger-side front fender and header panel. Forced off the road, the coupe retreated into storage. Having met Troy McCool (Dylan’s father) at regional car shows, Ball traded vehicles and parts with him for years. Over 20 years ago, Ball sold the 340 engine, fuel tank, and fuel lines to Troy.
Photo: YouTube/Dylan McCool Troy McCool installed that small-block motor into a 1970 Dodge Challenger, which he eventually sold to a friend who still owns the vehicle today. Meanwhile, Ball kept the engineless 1972 shell tucked indoors. With four grandchildren and a fifth grandchild on the way, shifting family priorities finally convinced Ball to pass the torch. He sold the Challenger to Dylan McCool, bringing the Mopar family history full circle after 25 years.
Despite sitting stationary for most of this millennium, the Challenger preserved its structural integrity remarkably well. The body retained much of its factory baby blue paint, complemented by a green replacement passenger fender, a primered Rally hood replacing the original flat hood, earlier 1970 or 1971 bumpers, and a rear ducktail spoiler from a Challenger T/A. Inside, Ball had converted the originally blue cabin to black using pristine original seats from yet another donor car.
Beneath the dust, the Dodge boasted rock-solid floor pans, clean frame rails, and only minimal corrosion on a rear quarter panel. Even without an engine under the hood, the chassis offered an enviable foundation for a revival. It still carried a rebuilt front suspension, a refreshed automatic transmission with an aftermarket loose-stall torque converter, long-tube headers feeding a 3-inch dual exhaust with Flowmaster mufflers, and an 8.75-inch rear axle housing.
Photo: YouTube/Dylan McCool To return the pony Dodge to the pavement, Dylan arrived with a trusted 360 cubic-inch small-block V8 that he had previously installed in his 1972 Dodge Dart Swinger in 2013. Built with a stock rotating assembly, stock cylinder heads, an air-gap intake manifold, and a mild Comp Cams XE268 camshaft, the engine required an externally balanced B&M flexplate torqued to 55 foot-pounds before being hoisted into the bay.
The YouTuber and his trusty sidekick, Briar, replaced the front transmission seal and wrestled the 360 V8 between the long-tube headers. After bolting on an Edelbrock carburetor, modifying the kickdown linkage, and correcting a Mallory Unilite distributor that was initially set 180 degrees out of phase, they fired the engine. The V8 roared to life with 50 pounds of oil pressure, expelling a quarter-century’s worth of mouse nests out the tail pipes. A literal shove scoop, as you can see in the video.
Rebuilding the fuel and cooling systems brought unexpected comedy when Dylan McCool realized the brand-new replacement gas tank had flown out of his pickup bed during the one-hour drive to the shop. Troy McCool drove to Stephens Performance for another new tank, while Dylan hand-bent a 3/8-inch aluminum fuel line and fitted a universal $150 eBay radiator.
Photo: YouTube/Dylan McCool Tapping the top of the bellhousing with a hammer resolved minor flexplate rubbing. It’s called “wrenching,” but it’s not really serious unless there’s a bit of hammering sprinkled into the fix.
Getting the Challenger to stop safely required two days of persistent labor in chilly weather. The pair installed a new master cylinder, a front brake caliper, two rear wheel cylinders inside the 10-inch drums, and fresh rubber brake hoses after heating seized fittings with a torch. Mounted on factory police steel wheels with dog-dish hubcaps, the coupe rolled into the sunlight with Eddie Ball happily behind the wheel once more, for one last dance.
Photo: YouTube/Dylan McCool After pressure-washing 25 years of grime off the baby blue body and securing the broken headlight panel, Dylan and Briar ventured out into 35-degree weather for a shakedown run. Although the dead vacuum booster demanded heavy leg effort on the brake pedal, the car halted reliably. Initially stuck in second gear due to excessive line pressure, the transmission shifted smoothly into third gear once Dylan loosened the kickdown linkage.
With the rally hood bolted down, Dylan McCool tackled the hour-long voyage home across four-lane highways and country back roads alike. Aided by its 2.76 rear gear ratio and tight steering, the 1972 Dodge Challenger cruised effortlessly between 60 mph and 65 mph. Aside from stiff rear air shocks and minor oil misting from the dipstick tube, the resurrected coupe completed the trip flawlessly.
